newsitem.title: USA: Sex bias case could cost U.S. $500 mln - attorney.
newsitem.headline: Sex bias case could cost U.S. $500 mln - attorney.

text.p: A decades-old sex discrimination case against Voice of America involving 1,100 women could ultimately cost the U.S. government half a billion dollars, a lawyer for the women said on Thursday.

"There has been at VOA a systemic, persistent bias against women in hiring," attorney Bruce Fredrickson said. "In many instances, the service chiefs made no bones about the fact that there were limited roles available to women at VOA."

The original lawsuit against the government-run radio agency dates back to 1974, alleging that VOA disciminated against women who applied for jobs from 1974 to 1984. In 1984, a federal judge found VOA, which produces programs in English and dozens of foreign languages, guilty of discrimination.

Fredrickson said the suit seeks back pay for the women, as well as retirement and other benefits the claimants would have received had they been hired or promoted at VOA. Such awards could mount to $500 million, he said in a telephone interview.
Asked whether it was possible that the claimants might reach a settlement with VOA, Fredrickson demurred and then referred that question to officials at the radio agency.
VOA officials had no comment on the case on Thursday.

The final phase of the case began in June 1996, when a spcial master, George Washington University law professor Stephen Saltzburg, began considering individual cases. So far he has dealt with 10 cases, agreeing that eight of the women had faced discrimination and awarding them a total of about $4.7 million, according to a source familiar with the matter.

However, VOA's lawyers have appealed every award and only one woman has received any money in the entire history of the case. Rose Kobylinksi got less than $20,000 when her case was settled in 1984, Fredrickson said.
He said the cases, now being considered at the rate of two or three a month, could go on "for the foreseeable future."
The class-action case has been something of a personal crusade for Fredrickson, who remembered it as the first case he filed as a lawyer in 1977.
